scenes.heading: Escape Analysis & Stack vs Heap
scenes.narration: Let's look at escape analysis and how Go decides whether each value lives on the cheap stack or the garbage-collected heap.

scenes.heading: Two places a value can live
items: Stack: per-goroutine, freed for free on return
Heap: shared, scanned and reclaimed by the GC
The compiler chooses at build time, not you
scenes.narration: Every value your program creates has to live somewhere. The stack is a small per-goroutine region reclaimed instantly when a function returns, so allocation there is essentially free. The heap is shared and managed by the garbage collector, so it costs an allocation now and scanning work later. You don't pick — the compiler does, using a static pass called escape analysis.

scenes.heading: How the compiler decides
steps: Trace where each value's address flows
Prove the lifetime stays in the frame
If proven, keep it on the stack
If not, mark it moved to heap
scenes.narration: Escape analysis traces how each value's address flows through the program. If the compiler can prove the address never outlives the current function's frame, the value stays on the stack. If it cannot prove that — say the address is returned, stored globally, boxed into an interface, or captured by a closure — the value escapes and is heap-allocated. It is a dataflow proof of lifetime, not a heuristic about whether you took a pointer.

scenes.heading: Returning a pointer to a local
scenes.narration: In C, returning the address of a local variable is a dangling-pointer bug. In Go it is perfectly safe. Escape analysis sees that the address of u leaves newUser's frame, so it promotes u to the heap automatically. The pointer is always valid; the only cost is one allocation. Run go build with gcflags dash m and you'll see the compiler print moved to heap for u.

scenes.text: Measure with -gcflags=-m and -benchmem; only chase escapes that hot paths prove matter.
scenes.narration: Most escapes don't matter. Profile first with gcflags dash m to see the decisions and benchmem to see allocations per operation, then remove only the escapes a hot path proves costly — returning values instead of pointers, avoiding interface boxing, or pooling with sync dot Pool.
